title: Punishment Happens After the Punch
author: Jo Lein
summary: A middle school administrator writing as Jo Lein responds to a parent's demand for harsher punishment after a school fight by reframing the entire premise: responsibility for student safety, she argues, is not the same thing as control over student behavior. She dismantles the intuitive 'kid fights, kid gets punished, kid learns' model by pointing out that most middle schoolers already know fighting is wrong — the failure isn't knowledge but the capacity to act on that knowledge under intense social pressure, embarrassment, or fear. Lein walks through the specific skills walking away actually requires (self-control, confidence, tolerance of embarrassment, trust that an adult will help) to argue these are teachable competencies, not innate traits punishment can install. Her explanation for asking families to reinforce the same message at home is that school messaging about de-escalation competes directly with peer and cultural messages telling kids not to be 'a snitch' or to hit back — a competition the school alone cannot win. The piece closes on a reframe useful well beyond classroom discipline: that shared responsibility for a child's wellbeing works not by one party seizing control, but by multiple adults each claiming 'this part is mine.'
points: Lein's reframe — 'Responsibility is not the same as control' — directly rebuts the common parental and administrative assumption that a school's duty to keep students safe implies it can (or should) control every student choice through punishment alone.

Her breakdown of what 'just walk away' actually demands of a twelve-year-old under peer pressure (self-control, confidence, tolerance of embarrassment, trust that an adult will help) reframes de-escalation as a taught skill set rather than a simple behavioral instruction.

The observation that school de-escalation messaging competes directly with peer and cultural scripts ('don't be a snitch,' 'hit them back') explains why consistent reinforcement from parents, not just stricter school punishment, is necessary for the message to land.
quotes: The fights at school are my responsibility. But here's the part I keep getting stuck on: Responsibility is not the same as control.
'You need harsher consequences' is one of those solutions that feels very satisfying. Kid fights. Kid gets punished. Kid learns. Problem solved.
Most kids know they aren't supposed to fight. Knowing is not usually the issue.
Doing what you know when you are mad, embarrassed, hurt, scared, or surrounded by fourteen other kids yelling OOOOHHHHH is an entirely different situation.
We have to acknowledge that walking away in that moment requires a whole lot: Self-control. Confidence. Perspective. The ability to tolerate embarrassment.
Don't let anybody disrespect you. If somebody hits you, hit them back. Don't be scared. Don't be a snitch. And then at school we're saying: Walk away. Find an adult. De-escalate.
You can be deeply responsible for someone and still not control every choice they make.
